title: Two wills (8.9–8.10)
hook: he wants to change and doesn't want to, at the same time
tomorrow: what did young Augustine ask God for, with a catch?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk of Egypt, two officials at Trier, and a professor's cry. Your line: the unlearned rise.

An alarm goes off at six. The same hand that could turn it off and get up hits snooze. Augustine noticed the strangeness of that in a garden in Milan. He wills his hand to move, and it moves, so fast you can hardly tell the order from the doing. He wills his own mind to want God, fully, and it won't. The body obeys at once. The will drags its feet.
screen: `THE SAME HAND HITS SNOOZE.` → `THE HAND OBEYS.` → `THE WILL DRAGS ITS FEET.`

segments.voice: The question is old: can one person want two things at once? Augustine's Latin puts it sharply: imperat animus corpori, et paretur statim; imperat animus sibi, et resistitur. The mind commands the body and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself and is resisted. His answer: the mind doesn't will with the whole of itself. If it did, it wouldn't need to give the order. So there are two wills, an old one held by habit and a new one only beginning. And here's his firm line: it was I who willed, and I who was unwilling. Not two strangers fighting inside him. One person, divided, and so one person who can be healed. A neighbor tradition sits close to this. The Jewish Mishnah reads the verse, in the JPS translation, "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart", and says: with all your heart means with both your inclinations, the good inclination and the evil one, the yetzer. The Mishnah and Augustine both see one person pulled two ways, and both bring the whole divided heart to God. One honest difference: Augustine calls the split a sickness that grace heals into one will. The Mishnah asks a person to love God with both inclinations, even the one that pulls the other way.
screen: `THE BODY OBEYS. THE MIND RESISTS.` · `IT WAS I, AND I.` · `THE MISHNAH: BOTH INCLINATIONS.` · `HEALED INTO ONE, OR BOTH FOR GOD?` · then, large: `TWO WILLS.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you both want and don't want to change. Give each will one plain sentence in your head, the one that wants it and the one that doesn't, then add a third: one small next step both could live with. If you pray, you can hold all three before God, as one person.
Two wills. Augustine's name for wanting and not wanting at once: one person, divided, not two strangers.
Two wills, one person: the split is yours, and so both halves can be brought to God. Go in peace.

howItsDone: Catholics bring this kind of divided heart to prayer and to the sacrament of confession, and some turn to Augustine's account in Confessions 8 for words.

fork.reveal: the Mishnah reads 'with all thy heart' as with both inclinations. Augustine, from his side, insists both wills are his: 'it was I.'

original.note: Latin for will; Augustine writes of an old will and a new one (Confessions 8.5).

what a scholar hears: 'imperat animus sibi, et resistitur' (8.9), Augustine's 'ego eram' against the Manichees' two natures (8.10), and, as a neighbor, the Mishnah's two inclinations on Deuteronomy 6:5 (Berakhot 9:5).

chat.says: talked to dad. half of me's packed for the visit, half won't leave abuela's kitchen. which is the real me?
options: Both. Augustine said it was I who willed and I who didn't. One you, pulled two ways, not a fake half.
The visit half. Augustine says the new will is the real self, and the old one is just habit to ignore.
Neither. Augustine says two opposite natures fight inside you, so go with whichever one wins.
chat.meaning: Augustine: 'it was I who willed, and I who was unwilling.' Two wills, one person, and that's why both halves can be brought and healed.

Mishnah.meaning: an early collection of Jewish law and teaching

yetzer.meaning: Hebrew: an inclination or impulse in a person

JPS.meaning: the Jewish Publication Society's English translation of the Hebrew Bible

Milan.meaning: the city in northern Italy where Augustine was living

notes: Latin quoted from 8.9.21: 'imperat animus corpori, et paretur statim; imperat animus sibi, et resistitur.' Confirm.

The hand that obeys comes from 8.8.20; the mind not willing wholly from 8.9.21; 'an old will and a new one' from 8.5.10; 'it was I who willed, and I who was unwilling' paraphrases 8.10.22 (ego eram qui volebam, ego qui nolebam). Confirm.

v3 wisdom shape and the unity thread: one question (can one person want two things at once?), Augustine's answer, then a neighbor in its own words and source: Deuteronomy 6:5 quoted from JPS 1917 ('thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart'), and Mishnah Berakhot 9:5 paraphrased (with all your heart: with both your inclinations, the good inclination and the evil inclination). One honest difference: Augustine calls the split a sickness healed by grace into one will; the Mishnah asks that God be loved with both inclinations. Ranks neither; never 'all the same' (a chat wrong option names the two-natures trap instead). A Jewish scholar should confirm the Mishnah paraphrase and that the difference is fairly put.
The yetzer gloss gives the general meaning 'inclination'; the Mishnah's terms are yetzer tov and yetzer ha-ra. Confirm.
The alarm-clock image is the writer's.
